q: You are bending the new genoa sheets onto the clew of the sail before leaving Lefkas. Which knot do you tie?
a: Bowline
o: Clove hitch
Reef knot
Rolling hitch
why: A bowline makes a fixed loop through the clew that will not slip and unties after use.

q: You have pulled down the first reef and are tying the reef points round the loose bundle of sail. Which knot?
a: Reef knot
o: Sheet bend
Clove hitch
Figure of eight
why: Binding round a bundle is the reef knot's proper job: it lies flat and unties easily.

q: You are on the foredeck as this line starts to run. Where do you put your feet?
a: Outside the loop, clear of the line
o: Inside the loop, to hold it down on deck
On the line, to stop it running out
Anywhere, as the line is still slack
why: A bight snaps tight the instant the line takes up: never stand in one.

fig.title: Leaving the quay
lines: Stern line paying out across the deck
A loop of slack lies round your feet
Engine in gear, boat moving off

q: You are holding the dinghy painter while the crew climbs down, and the dinghy is pulling in the current. How do you hold the line?
a: In your hands, not wrapped round them
o: Wrapped once round your hand for a better grip
Looped round your wrist for grip
Tied round your waist to free your hands
why: A wrapped line can trap your hand and drag you if the load surges.

q: Your crew will handle sheets and mooring lines this afternoon. What should they wear on their hands?
a: Sailing gloves against rope burn
o: Nothing: bare hands grip better
Thick woollen gloves for padding
One glove on the hand that tails
why: Sailing gloves protect palms from rope burn while keeping a good grip.

fig.title: Meltemi afternoon
lines: Stern-to in a crowded harbour tonight

q: What do you do with the mooring lines before you stow them?
a: Rinse in fresh water, then dry them
o: Stow them wet, salt and all, to keep them soft
Dry them in the sun without rinsing
Scrub them clean with bleach
why: Salt crystals cut the fibres and stiffen rope; rope stowed wet goes mouldy.

fig.title: Charter handover, Saturday
lines: Lines go back into the cockpit locker

q: The cut end of a new polyester sheet has started to unravel. What do you do?
a: Whip the end and seal it with heat
o: Tie an overhand knot in the end to stop it
Wrap insulating tape round it
Wet the end to swell the fibres
why: Whipping binds the end and heat fuses the synthetic fibres so it cannot fray.

q: You have finished winching in the genoa sheet. What do you do with the winch handle?
a: Take it out and stow it
o: Leave it in the winch for the next tack
Lay it on the cockpit seat
Hang it over the guardrail
why: A handle left in fouls the sheets, gets kicked overboard or injures someone.

q: Six clutches sit side by side on the coachroof. Before you open one to drop the main, you…
a: check its label and follow the line
o: open the one nearest the companionway
open each in turn until it moves
take the turns off the winch first
why: Opening the wrong clutch can drop a loaded line such as the kicker or a reef line.

q: You are reversing onto the quay in Poros and a long slack loop of the stern line hangs over the transom into the water. What is the risk?
a: It can wrap round the propeller
o: It will stretch and lose strength
It acts as a brake on the stern
It will float away from the boat
why: Keep lines on deck and out of the water whenever the engine is in gear.

q: Your crew has led the bow line straight over the toerail to the cleat. What should they do?
a: Lead it through the fairlead first
o: Leave it, the toerail is smooth
Tie it round the pulpit instead
Add a second line over the toerail
why: A fairlead gives a smooth lead; a toerail edge chafes the line.

q: You want a quiet night and less wear on the lines. What do you do?
a: Tie them off away from the mast
o: Ease the halyards so they hang slack
Take the shackles off and let them swing free
Leave them; the noise does no harm
why: Tied off away from the mast, halyards stop slapping and chafing.

q: You are hauling in the mainsheet where it runs into the block on the traveller. Where do you keep your hands?
a: Well back from the block
o: Right up at the block for the best grip
On the block itself, guiding the line in
Either side of the sheave
why: A sudden load can drag fingers into the block.

q: What do you tell the charter base about this sheet?
a: It needs replacing before you sail
o: It is fine while the core is still intact
Tape over the worn part and sail
Turn it so the wear is underneath
why: Once the cover is through, the core chafes fast and the sheet can part.

fig.title: Pre-charter check
lines: Genoa sheet: cover worn through at clew

q: You are about to throw the stern line to a helper on the pontoon. What do you do with the other end first?
a: Make it fast to the cleat on board
o: Throw it as well, so they have both
Leave it loose on the deck
Tie it round your wrist
why: If the inboard end is made fast, the whole line cannot go overboard.

q: A tired swimmer beside the boat needs a loop under the arms to help them up the stern ladder. Which knot?
a: Bowline
o: Running bowline
Slip knot
Clove hitch
why: A bowline's loop is fixed: it will not tighten round the chest.

q: You are tying the sail ties round the flaked mainsail and want each one to come off with one pull when you next hoist. Which knot?
a: Slipped reef knot
o: Reef knot pulled tight
Clove hitch
Double sheet bend
why: The slipped loop releases the knot with a single tug.

q: You are buying a spare mooring line for an Ionian charter, where you will often lie stern-to in a swell. Which material?
a: Nylon
o: Polyester
Polypropylene
Dyneema
why: Nylon stretches and absorbs the surge before it reaches the cleats.

q: You are bending a nylon warp straight onto the ring of the kedge anchor. Which knot?
a: Anchor bend
o: Clove hitch
Reef knot
Double sheet bend
why: The anchor (fisherman's) bend nips tight on the ring and will not shake loose.

q: Overnight, the clove hitch on the bollard has worked loose as the boat surged. What should you have tied?
a: Round turn and two half hitches
o: Reef knot
Slipped reef knot
Sheet bend
why: The round turn takes the surge and the half hitches stay locked; a clove hitch can roll loose.

q: The single sheet bend joining these two lines keeps working loose. What do you tie instead?
a: Double sheet bend
o: Reef knot
Clove hitch
Slipped reef knot
why: The extra turn of a double sheet bend grips slippery or very unequal lines.

q: You want a stopper knot in the end of the mainsheet that you can still undo after it has been jerked hard against the block. Which knot?
a: Figure of eight
o: Overhand knot
Double overhand knot
Reef knot
why: A figure of eight is bulky enough to stop and does not jam like an overhand.

q: Tying the reef points, your crew passes left over right, then left over right again. What has she tied?
a: A granny, which can slip or jam
o: A reef knot, ready to use
A sheet bend, for unequal ropes
A clove hitch, for a rail
why: Right over left then left over right makes a reef knot; the same way twice makes a granny.

q: Your crew has made the stern line fast with three locking hitches piled on top of the cleat. What is wrong?
a: It can jam and be slow to release
o: Nothing, more hitches hold better
It needs another turn round the base
It should have been a bowline
why: One locking hitch is enough; more of them jam just when you need to let go.

q: You are making the stern line fast on a pontoon cleat. Where does the line go first?
a: Far horn first, then a turn round the base
o: Straight into a locking hitch on the near horn
Into figure-of-eight turns with no turn first
Round the near horn, then over the top
why: Leading to the far horn first lets the base turn take the load without the line trapping itself.

q: The stern line is loaded and you need to ease it by a metre. How do you do it?
a: Keep one turn on and let it slip round
o: Take it off the cleat and hold it by hand
Pull the locking hitch tighter first
Lift the whole lot off the horns at once
why: The turn round the base holds the load while you ease under control.

q: Your crew is on the pontoon holding the bow line, and the wind is blowing the boat off. She cannot hold it. What does she do?
a: Take a turn round the cleat
o: Dig in and pull with both hands
Wrap the line round her wrist
Run along the pontoon with it
why: A turn round a cleat gives the grip no person has; a yacht cannot be held by hand.

q: You are tacking in light air and pulling the new genoa sheet in fast by hand. How many turns are on the winch?
a: Two, adding more as the load comes on
o: Four from the start, so it cannot slip
None until the sail is fully in
One, then the rest with the handle
why: Few turns let the slack come in fast without riding turns; add turns as the load builds.

q: The helm calls "Lee-oh" and you must let the old genoa sheet go. How?
a: Pull the tail free, lift the turns off
o: Unwind the turns one at a time
Leave it on the winch to pull itself free
Take the handle out and spin the drum back
why: Flicking the turns up off the drum releases the sheet at once so the sail can cross.

q: You are loading the sheet onto a self-tailing winch. What is the order?
a: Clockwise turns, then over the arm into the jaws
o: Straight into the jaws with no turns on the drum
Turns anticlockwise, then into the jaws
One turn, then hold the tail by hand
why: The drum turns do the gripping; the jaws only hold the tail.

q: You are tailing while a crew member grinds the genoa in. What is your job?
a: Pull the tail steadily so the turns grip
o: Hold the tail loosely and let the winch work
Push the turns up the drum as they come in
Grind as well with your other hand
why: Tension on the tail is what makes the turns grip the drum.

q: You need to ease the loaded genoa sheet a few centimetres on a plain winch. How?
a: Keep the turns on and ease them round
o: Take all the turns off and let it run
Wind the handle backwards a little
Uncleat it and let go of the tail
why: With the turns kept on, the drum's friction lets you ease under control.

q: The main halyard is loaded and you want to ease it. What do you do first?
a: Load the winch, then open the clutch
o: Open the clutch, then put it on the winch
Open the clutch and hold the tail by hand
Open the clutch and let it run to the mark
why: With the load on the winch the clutch opens gently and the line cannot run away.

fig.title: Main halyard
lines: Winch beside the clutch is free

q: You have hoisted the main on the coachroof winch. What do you do before you take the turns off the winch?
a: Make sure the halyard clutch is closed
o: Ease the halyard a little first
Cleat the tail on the winch top
Open the clutch to check it runs
why: The closed clutch holds the halyard so the winch is free for the next line.

q: What do you replace it with?
a: Low-stretch polyester or Dyneema braid
o: New nylon three-strand of the same size
Polypropylene braid, which is light
A thicker nylon braid for strength
why: Halyards need low stretch to hold luff tension; nylon stretches.

q: The charter boat's genoa sheets have been replaced with nylon. What will you notice?
a: The sail eases itself in every gust
o: Nothing: nylon is ideal for sheets
They float and trail in the water
They are too stiff to go round a winch
why: Nylon stretches; sheets need low-stretch polyester.

q: Why has this line aged so fast?
a: Polypropylene breaks down in sunlight
o: Salt water slowly dissolves polypropylene
It was always coiled the wrong way
It has soaked up too much water
why: Polypropylene has poor UV resistance; check it and replace it often.

fig.title: Dinghy painter
lines: Snaps when you bend it hard

q: You want to splice an eye into a new mooring line yourself, on board, with only a knife and tape. Which construction is easiest?
a: Three-strand
o: Double-braid polyester
Braid with a Dyneema core
Braid-on-braid nylon
why: Three-strand is spliced by tucking strands by hand; braid needs fids and skill.

q: What has caused this?
a: Friction heat has melted the fibres
o: Salt has crystallised in the cover
The sun has bleached the cover
Oil from the winch has soaked in
why: A line surging fast round a drum heats up enough to glaze synthetic fibres.

fig.title: Halyard inspection
lines: Hard, shiny patch on the cover
Where it surged round the winch

q: This line is bar taut in a gust. Where do you stand?
a: To one side, out of line with it
o: Right behind it, to watch it
Astride it, ready to hold it down
Next to the bollard, to check it
why: A stretched nylon line that parts whips back along its own path.

fig.note: Nylon stern line under heavy load

q: Where the stern line crosses the quay edge it rubs every time the boat moves. What do you do?
a: Fit a chafe sleeve at the edge
o: Tighten it until it stops moving
Tie a knot at the rubbing point
Wet it now and then to cool it
why: A hose or chafe guard takes the wear instead of the rope.

fig.title: Stern-to, stone quay
lines: Stern line running over the edge

q: You need to cut a 10 m length off a new coil of braided polyester. How?
a: Tape it, cut through the tape, heat-seal
o: Cut it with a knife and whip the ends next week
Burn through it with a lighter alone
Cut it, then tie an overhand knot in each end
why: Tape stops the braid unravelling as you cut; heat then fuses the ends.

q: You are coiling a three-strand mooring line. Which way do you lay the loops?
a: Clockwise, with the lay
o: Anticlockwise, against the lay
Round your elbow, either way
Either way, lay does not matter
why: Most three-strand is right-hand laid; coil it clockwise to avoid kinks.

q: A braided sheet keeps forming twists when you coil it in round loops. What works better?
a: Lay it in figure-of-eight loops
o: Coil it tighter and faster
Coil it anticlockwise instead
Wet it first so it lies flat on deck
why: Braid has no lay; figure-of-eight loops put no twist into it.

q: After hoisting, you have coiled the halyard tail from this cleat. How do you hang it?
a: Pull a loop through the coil, twist it, hang it
o: Leave the coil lying loose on the deck by the mast
Wrap the tail round the whole coil and drop it
Tie the coil to the guardrail with its own end
why: The hung coil stays tidy and lifts off ready to run.

q: You are coiling a mooring line that is still made fast on the cleat. Where do you start?
a: At the cleat, working out to the free end
o: At the free end, working back to the cleat
In the middle, working both ways
Anywhere, as long as the loops are equal
why: Twists then run out of the free end instead of building up in the coil.

q: What do you check before opening the halyard clutch?
a: The tail is flaked and free to run
o: The tail is made fast on a cleat
The tail is tied to the boom
The tail is coiled and hung up
why: A kinked or knotted tail jams at the clutch and leaves the sail half down.

fig.title: Dropping the main
lines: Halyard tail in a heap in the cockpit
Boat head to wind under engine

q: After a season, the genoa sheets are starting to wear where they run through the fairleads. What do you do?
a: Swap each sheet end for end
o: Throw them both away
Tape over the worn part
Swap the port and starboard sheets
why: End-for-ending moves the wear to a fresh part of the rope.

q: You are making up a permanent mooring line with a loop in one end. Why splice the eye rather than tie a bowline?
a: It keeps more of the rope's strength
o: A splice is quicker to undo
A bowline cannot go over a bollard
A splice lets you change the loop size
why: A knot weakens a rope far more than a well-made splice.

q: You are shackling a rope warp to a length of chain. What goes inside the eye splice?
a: A thimble, to protect the eye
o: Nothing, the splice is strong enough
A knot, to stop it pulling through
Tape, to help it slide on the shackle
why: The metal thimble spreads the load and protects the eye from chafe.

q: You are throwing the bow line to a helper on the pontoon. Where do you aim?
a: Above and just beyond them
o: Straight at their chest
At their feet on the pontoon
Short, into the water by them
why: A line aimed past the person drops across them; one aimed at them falls short.

q: Your thrown stern line falls short into the water between the boat and the quay. What now?
a: Pull it in fast, clear of the prop
o: Throw the rest of the line out after it
Motor astern so the helper can reach it
Leave it there and throw the other line
why: A line in the water near the stern can foul the prop; recover it first.

q: The marinero has done this with your stern line. Where is it adjusted and made fast?
a: On the boat's cleat, by your crew
o: On the bollard, by the marinero
With a bowline round the bollard
Held by hand until the engine stops
why: Made fast on board, the line can be adjusted or slipped without going ashore.

fig.note: Line taken round the bollard, end handed back

q: The quay is too far to throw the heavy stern line. What do you do?
a: Throw a light line first to pull it across
o: Throw the heavy line again, much harder
Tie both stern lines together and throw them
Throw the coil without holding the end
why: A light heaving line carries further; the heavy line follows it.

q: How do you rig the stern line so you can let go from on board?
a: Both ends aboard, middle round the bollard
o: A bowline round the bollard, end on board
A clove hitch on the bollard, end on board
Round turn and two half hitches ashore
why: A slip line is released from aboard by letting one end go and pulling in the other.

q: You are letting go a slip line from the stern. What must be true before you put the engine in gear?
a: The whole line is back aboard
o: One end is let go and trailing
The line is bar tight on the cleat
The free end is thrown onto the quay
why: A slip line trailing astern can wrap the prop the moment it turns.

q: You are lashing the upturned dinghy on the foredeck and want the lashing bar tight. Which hitch?
a: Trucker's hitch
o: Round turn and two half hitches
Clove hitch
Reef knot
why: The loop in a trucker's hitch works like a pulley, giving purchase to tension the line.

q: You must cast off this line while the boat is still pulling on it. How?
a: Undo the hitches while the turn holds the load
o: Wait until the load comes off it first
Cut it, as the hitches will be jammed
Pull the whole knot off the ring at once
why: The round turn takes the strain while the half hitches are undone.

fig.note: Round turn and two half hitches, under load

q: You are stowing a spare line in the cockpit locker. How do you keep it from tangling?
a: Coil it, bind it, tuck the end through
o: Stuff it in loose so it can breathe
Knot both ends together and drop it in
Leave it flaked loose on the locker floor
why: A bound coil stays together and is ready to use.

q: How do you get the stern line in?
a: Lead it to a winch and grind it in
o: Two people pull and hold it by hand
Tie it to the next boat's cleat
Motor ahead to slacken the line
why: A winch gives the purchase that hands cannot; keep a fair lead to the drum.

fig.title: Stern-to, crosswind
lines: Windward stern line on the quay bollard
Too heavy to pull in by hand

q: A loaded mooring line starts running out fast through your hands. What do you do?
a: Let it go and regain it with a turn on a cleat
o: Grip harder with both hands until it stops
Wrap it round your wrist for more grip
Stand on it to stop it running
why: Gripping a running line burns hands; a turn on a cleat stops it safely.

q: Why does this shorten the life of the lines?
a: Grit cuts the fibres from inside
o: Sand makes the lines float
Being walked on stretches them
It only marks the cover, no harm done
why: Sand and grit grind the fibres from inside; keep lines off the ground.

fig.title: Charter base quay
lines: Mooring lines left on the sandy quay

q: You are grinding the genoa in and this is happening. What do you do?
a: Add another turn on the drum
o: Grind faster to keep up with it
Take a turn off the drum
Let the tail go slack
why: More turns give more friction; under heavy load the drum needs three or four.

fig.note: Sheet creeping round the drum, 22 kn

q: You are about to throw a coiled stern line. How do you hold the coil?
a: Split: half to throw, half to pay out
o: The whole coil in your throwing hand
Wound round your forearm
Tied together with its own end
why: The thrown loops carry the line while the rest runs free from the other hand.

q: The genoa sheet is getting too heavy to grind on the two-speed winch. What do you do?
a: Turn the handle the other way
o: Take a turn off the drum
Let the tail go and grind faster
Put more turns on and grind harder
why: Reversing the handle on a two-speed winch selects the lower, more powerful gear.

q: You need to release the mainsheet from its cam cleat. How?
a: Pull in slightly, then lift it out
o: Push it down deeper into the cams
Pull it sideways against the cams
Let go and wait for it to slip free
why: A small pull takes the load off the cams so the line lifts out.

q: You are joining a thin line to a thick one with a sheet bend. Which line forms the U-shaped bight?
a: The thicker line
o: The thinner line
Either, it makes no difference
Both, laid side by side
why: The thick line makes the bight and the thin line wraps round it.

q: After a week of use, the three-strand stern line is full of kinks. How do you get them out?
a: Lay it out and work twists out of the end
o: Coil it tighter to press the kinks out
Soak it in fresh water overnight to relax it
Leave it coiled in the sun to soften
why: Twist must run out of an end; coiling or soaking just traps it.

q: Your crew has long loose hair and a scarf and is about to grind the halyard winch. What do you say?
a: Tie the hair back, tuck the scarf away
o: Keep the scarf on against the sun
Stand further back from the drum while grinding
Wear gloves and carry on
why: Hair and loose clothing can be wound into a turning drum.

q: A heavy stern line is under strain round a big bollard ashore. You must hold it, ease it under control, then cast it off with the load still on. Which hitch?
a: Lighterman's hitch
o: Bowline
Clove hitch
Double sheet bend
why: The lighterman's (tugboat) hitch holds a heavy load on a post and still releases under strain.

q: Your bow line is tied to the quay ring with a bowline, and the wind presses the boat off so it is bar tight. You want to leave. What is the problem?
a: A loaded bowline cannot be untied
o: The bowline will slip through the ring
The bowline capsizes when touched
Nothing: a bowline frees under load
why: A bowline holds well but the load must come off before it can be untied.

fig.note: Bowline, wind pressing the boat off

q: A crew member has loaded the genoa sheet like this. What happens when the sail fills?
a: The sheet runs out round the drum
o: It holds, but grinding is much harder
The winch locks and cannot be eased
Nothing, the direction does not matter
why: Yacht winches only hold one way; the turns must go on clockwise.

q: How much load should you plan to put on it?
a: About a fifth of that, at most
o: Up to the full 3,800 kg
About 3,000 kg, a 20% margin
About half, 1,900 kg
why: Safe working load allows for knots, wear and shock, so it is far below breaking strength.

fig.title: New mooring line
lines: Will be knotted and run over a quay edge

q: A crew member ties a bowline in uncovered Dyneema to lift the outboard onto the pushpit. Why are you wary?
a: Knots can slip in it; splice it
o: It stretches too much under load
It is too weak for an outboard
It sinks if dropped over the side
why: Dyneema is slippery and many knots creep in it, so it is spliced for loads.

q: Your crew offers this line for the windward stern line. What is the problem?
a: No stretch, so surges snatch the cleats
o: It is too weak to be used as a mooring line
It sinks and chafes on the seabed
It cannot be tied to a bollard
why: Mooring lines need stretch; Dyneema passes shock loads straight to the fittings.

fig.title: Stern-to, Kos harbour
lines: Swell rolling in from the gap

q: Why did it part?
a: Snatch loads far above the steady pull
o: The wind rose by a few knots
The line was too stretchy
Wet rope always loses half its strength
why: Shock loads can be many times the steady load; stretch and snubbers absorb them.

fig.title: Town quay, Vis
lines: Swell arrived: boat surging, lines snatching
One stern line parted at 3 am

q: The chain hook on your snubber has gone over the side. You want to tie the nylon snubber line onto the anchor chain so it takes the pull along the chain. Which knot?
a: Rolling hitch
o: Clove hitch
Bowline
Double sheet bend
why: A rolling hitch grips when pulled along the chain; a clove hitch slides.

q: You need to put your own loop on this bollard. How?
a: Up through their loop, then over the top
o: Drop your loop over the top of theirs
Lift theirs off and put yours on first
Tie your loop to theirs with a bowline
why: Dipping the eye lets either boat lift its loop off without disturbing the other.

fig.note: Another boat's loop is already on it

q: You rig a slip line through a quay ring. Your crew wants to tie a bowline in the end that will run through the ring. Why not?
a: The knot can jam in the ring
o: A bowline weakens the line too much
It is harder to make fast on board
The bowline will shake itself undone
why: A slip line must run free; any knot or eye can snag the ring.

fig.note: Slip line: both ends on board

q: You arrive for two nights on the town quay and plan an early start. When do you rig the stern lines as slip lines?
a: Just before leaving, not on arrival
o: On arrival, to save time later
Never: only when single-handed
Only if the marinero asks you to
why: Both parts of a slip line move and chafe; rig it just before you go.

q: You keep getting riding turns on this winch. How should the sheet lead onto the drum?
a: From slightly below the drum
o: From well above, sloping down onto it
Level with the top of the drum
From any angle, it makes no difference
why: A lead from slightly below makes each new turn go on under the others.

q: Your new halyard, one size thinner than the old one, creeps through the closed clutch under load. Why?
a: The clutch suits the old diameter
o: Clutches only grip nylon line
The clutch needs oiling
The halyard is led the wrong way
why: Clutch jaws grip a set range of diameters; thinner or slicker rope slips.

q: Leaving the dinghy astern overnight, a crew member ties the painter with a slipped hitch so it is quick to free. Why is this a poor choice?
a: A tug or a snag can release it
o: Slipped hitches jam solid when wet
A slipped hitch cannot go on a cleat
It weakens the painter by half
why: Slipped knots are for quick release while attended, not unattended loads.

fig.title: Overnight at anchor
lines: Dinghy towed astern on its painter
Wind expected to rise after midnight
Painter on the stern rail, slipped hitch

q: You have agreed to tow a disabled yacht into Göcek. Which of your lines do you use for the tow?
a: The long nylon line, for its stretch
o: The Dyneema spare, as it is strongest
A polyester sheet, as it is stiff
The polypropylene line, as it floats
why: A long, stretchy tow absorbs the snatching between the two boats.

q: You are kitting out your own yacht. Which set of rope choices is right?
a: Nylon warp, polyester sheets, polypropylene painter
o: Polyester warp, nylon sheets, polypropylene painter
Nylon warp, polypropylene sheets, polyester painter
Polypropylene warp, polyester sheets, nylon painter
why: Stretch for the warp, low stretch for sheets, floating rope for the painter.

q: You have your finger on the winch button. What now?
a: Stop it and find the snag
o: Keep the button pressed until it frees
Add another turn and keep going
Switch to the faster speed
why: An electric winch can break gear or crush hands; look before you pull.

fig.title: Hoisting the main
lines: Sail stops 2 m below the masthead

q: You need to ease the loaded sheet on a self-tailing winch. What do you do first?
a: Take the tail out of the jaws
o: Ease it while it stays in the jaws
Take all the turns off the drum
Push the turns down with the handle
why: Out of the jaws, you control the tail and the drum turns do the easing.

q: The spring and the stern line share one cleat, with the stern line on top. Why is this a problem when you leave?
a: The spring is trapped under the stern line
o: The cleat cannot take the load of two lines
The stern line will slip off the spring
Two lines must be tied together first
why: The line underneath is trapped until the one on top is taken off.

labels: spring under, stern line on top

q: This line takes a hard snatch in a gust and parts. Where is it most likely to break?
a: At the bowline, its weakest point
o: Halfway along, where the load is
At the cleat on board
Anywhere, all points are equal
why: The tight bends in a knot weaken a rope far more than a smooth turn or a splice.

fig.note: Bowline on the bollard, cleated on board

q: Your crew wants to take a loaded sheet off a winch by unwinding it from the drum one turn at a time. Why do you stop them?
a: The line can run away as turns come off
o: Unwinding damages the winch ratchet
It puts a twist into the sheet each time
The drum will spin backwards
why: Under load, ease with all turns on, or flick them off together with hands clear.
